The cash cost of caregiving: combine support bills, lost earnings and available help

A dated Canadian survey graphic and three interactive scenarios show how paid help, reduced earnings, setup costs and existing budget capacity affect cash needs.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Add transport/supplies and the reduction in net earnings, then subtract confirmed net support and the household’s pre-care monthly budget surplus. Setup cost is paid at time zero; recurring net amounts settle at month-end. The central idea

An unpaid care role can affect a budget through both extra bills and reduced earnings. Build one incremental cash ledger, then compare its timing with the money actually available.

01

Use survey context without treating it as a personal forecast

Statistics Canada’s 2022 survey, published in April 2024, reports mutually exclusive shares of 58.1% with no unpaid care, 14.4% providing adult care only, 21.9% child care only and 5.6% both. The target population was non-institutionalized people aged 15 or older living off-reserve in the ten provinces; the reference was care in the previous twelve months.

The first graphic displays those rounded survey estimates. It remains fixed when scenario inputs change. The source provides confidence intervals; the chart does not estimate an individual’s future care needs or the price of paid help.

The other three graphics are hypothetical cash calculations for a selected arrangement. Their hours, hourly cost, earnings reduction and support amounts are editable assumptions. They are not estimates derived from the survey.

02

Add both sides of the household cash impact

Start with the budget before the new arrangement. The model takes the monthly surplus already left after that budget, then calculates what the care arrangement changes. Paid support and additional transport or supplies add outflows. A reduction in net earnings removes receipts even though it is not a bill from a provider.

The default eight hours of paid support each week at CAD 35 per hour becomes CAD 1,213.33 per average month, using 52 weeks divided by twelve. Add CAD 150 of transport and supplies and CAD 800 of lower monthly net earnings. The combined incremental burden is CAD 2,163.33.

Confirmed net support of CAD 300 and the existing CAD 500 monthly budget surplus reduce the amount drawn from cash to CAD 1,363.33 per month. The waterfall makes these offsets visible so a source of help is not accidentally deducted twice or counted before it is available.

03

Place one-time expenses at the start

The default arrangement also requires CAD 2,000 at setup. That amount is paid before the recurring monthly flows begin. The reserve path therefore starts at CAD 10,000 after setup from the selected CAD 12,000 starting reserve.

At the selected monthly draw, the illustrative cash position is still positive after month seven and negative after month eight. The negative section represents unfunded cash needs. It does not assume a bank permits an overdraft, a family member lends money, or a provider allows payment to be postponed.

Across twenty-four months, setup plus recurring net draws requires CAD 34,720 of starting cash under the model. After counting the CAD 12,000 already allocated, the additional amount is CAD 22,720. These figures use the unrounded monthly arithmetic; displayed values may be rounded to cents.

04

Use support amounts that can actually fund the schedule

The support input is a net receipt that is assumed available every month. It does not calculate a tax credit, employer benefit, public program payment or reimbursement. A benefit paid later cannot fund an earlier invoice unless another source covers the interval.

Keep the earnings reduction consistent with the starting budget. If the base budget already uses the lower earnings, adding the same reduction again would overstate the burden. Similarly, enter only additional travel and supplies, rather than costs already included in regular household spending.

A negative monthly draw means entered resources exceed the incremental recurring burden. Even then, setup still needs funding at time zero. The required-starting-cash measure therefore cannot fall below the setup amount merely because later monthly receipts replenish cash.

05

Vary the arrangement and revisit the wider plan

The matrix compares paid support hours and durations while holding other selected inputs fixed. Each cell reports the additional starting cash after the chosen reserve. It is a funding comparison, rather than a determination of how many care hours are suitable.

Different arrangements may also change the caregiver’s earnings, travel or support eligibility. The fixed-grid comparison isolates hours and duration, so those related effects must be considered separately. A new quote or confirmed work schedule provides a reason to update the inputs.

The model does not put a monetary value on all unpaid work, calculate lost pension contributions, assess health needs or evaluate care quality. Those questions require their own information. The ledger’s purpose is narrower and practical: identify which receipts change, which bills arrive, when setup must be paid and whether available cash covers the selected schedule.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
